Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the history of research ethics and some of the major ethical violations that have
occurred in the history of medical research.
Determine how ethical violations lead to evolutions in medical research ethics practices and
regulations.
Identify the ethical framework in which a current medical research study should be crafted
and conducted.
History of Medical Ethics
Cuba and Walter Reed
One of the first medical ethics controversies that meaningfully impacted how the United States
conducts medical research originated in Cuba in the late 1800s.1-3

To determine the etiology of yellow fever, Giuseppe Sanarelli injected a microbe he suspected
was the cause into five people, leading to serious harm to the individuals and wide criticism.1-3
In response, the Surgeon General of the United States instructed Walter Reed, MD, to discover
the cause of yellow fever.
After receiving this commission, Dr. Reed developed a set of ethical guidelines that the project
would follow.
A United States Army Yellow Fever Board was created to implement and ensure adherence to
the guidelines; this board currently is considered the foundation of the research ethics
committee.1,2
Nazis, War Crimes, and the Nuremburg Code
In the mid 1900s, physicians in Nazi concentration camps infamously performed grotesque,
abusive, and sadistic medical experiments on unwilling subjects, resulting in the death and
mutilation of many individuals, primarily Jewish individuals, Russians, Poles, prisoners of war,
and Romanies.4,5
After the war, these horrific crimes came to light. The first two Nuremburg war crimes
tribunals were called the Doctors’ Trials.4,5
During these tribunals, physicians and administrators who were responsible for these
atrocities were tried, and some were sentenced to capital punishment or long
imprisonment.4,5
The judicial members of the Nuremberg tribunal then went a step further and developed the
Nuremburg Code (Table 1), which was a major advancement in established medical and
research ethics.4,5
Table 1
The Nuremberg Code: A 10-Point Statement Delimiting Permissible Medical
Experimentation on Human Subjects
1. The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.
2. The experiment should be such as to yield fruitful results for the good of society,
unprocurable by other methods or means of study, and not random and unnecessary in
nature.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
2/19

3. The experiment should be based on animal experimentation...and the natural history of
the disease...anticipated results will justify the performance of the experiment.
4. The experiment should be so conducted as to avoid all unnecessary physical and mental
suffering and injury.
5. No experiment should be conducted in which a reason exists to believe that death or
disabling injury will occur.
6. The degree of risk to be taken should never exceed...the importance of the problem to be
solved by the experiment.
7. Proper preparations should be made...to protect the experimental subject against even
remote possibilities of injury, disability, or death.
8. The experiment should be conducted only by scientifically qualified persons.
9. During the experiment, the human subject should be at liberty to bring the experiment to
an end...
10. During the experiment, the scientist in charge must be prepared to terminate the
experiment at any stage if probable cause exists to believe...that a continuation of the
experiment is likely to result in injury, disability, or death to the experimental subject.
Based on Trials of War Criminals before the Nuremberg Military Tribunals Under Control Council
LawNo. 10. Washington, DC, United States Government Printing Office, 1949, vol 2, pp 181-182.
The major elements of the Nuremburg Code included emphasizing absolute requirements for
voluntary consent and withdrawal by the research subject, protection of the subject from
harm, and confirmation of the competency and responsibilities of the researchers4,6-8
(Resource 1).
Declaration of Helsinki
Two decades later, the World Medical Association organized the Nuremberg Code into a series
of ethical principles known as the Declaration of Helsinki, which has been revised frequently
and has influenced the conduct of clinical research for many years4,7,9 (Resource 2). A
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
3/19

resolution adopted by the World Medical Association held that “Under no circumstances is a
doctor permitted to do anything which would weaken the physical or mental resistance of a
human being except from strictly therapeutic or prophylactic indications imposed by the
interest of the patient.”4,10
United States Codifications (1950s–1960s)
In the mid 1950s, the Clinical Center of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) established
guidelines that were based directly on the Nuremberg Code and that were required to be
applied for standard volunteers and research.4,5
The NIH and the FDA then created a more extensive set of regulations.4,11
In 1966, the NIH established a policy of approving funding for research with human subjects
only if the grantee institution provided prior review of its research methods and an analysis of
the risks and advantages of the research protocol.4,5,11
Continued Ethical Abuses and Changes in Law
Despite efforts to require medical research to be conducted ethically, severely unethical
studies continued to be conducted.4,5,10
These morally unsound projects included, but were not limited to, studies that took place
without informed consent and that often resulted in substantial risk and/or harm to the
human subjects.4,5,10
Plutonium injections by Manhattan Project physicians (1945–1947)
Radioactive iodine and other isotope administration experiments by the Atomic Energy
Commission (1950–1970)
Radiation experiments in the Marshall Islands (1954)
Central Intelligence Agency studies of hallucinogens (1953) and pertussis (1955)
The Willowbrook Experiments on psychiatric patients (1965)
The exposure of United States service personnel to atomic radiation tests (1940–1971)
One of the most egregious studies was the Tuskegee Syphilis Experiment (1932–1972), which
observed the progression of unmanaged syphilis in poor African American men despite an
available treatment option.4,12-14
The series of ethical abuses in human subjects research, particularly the Tuskegee Syphilis
Experiment, led Congress to pass the National Research Act (1974). This act created the
National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
4/19

Research, which was tasked to articulate ethical principles and develop guidelines for human
subjects research.1,4,15
After 4 years of discussions, the Commission published, Ethical Principles and Guidelines for the
Protection of Human Subjects of Research, also known as the Belmont Report (1979).1,4,15
The Belmont Report defined research as being distinct from clinical practice. Clinical practice
was defined as an intervention solely for the purpose of providing diagnosis, preventive
treatment, or therapy to an individual, whereas research was designed to test hypotheses and
create information generalizable to the population at large.1,4,15
The report delineated three fundamental ethical principles for human subjects research:
respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.1,4,15
Respect for persons stipulated that individuals should be considered as autonomous agents
and required informed consent for participation in research.1,4,15
Beneficence, from a research standpoint, meant that the study design should optimize the
advantages from the project while minimizing risks to the subjects involved.1,4,15
Justice meant that the procedures of the study should be supported by sound reasoning, not
be exploitative in nature, and be conducted fairly.1,4,15
Shortly after the publication of the Belmont Report, the US Department of Health & Human
Services updated its regulations to align with the principles articulated in the report.1,4,15
In 1981, the principles of respect for persons, beneficence, and justice were codified into law
through the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) as the “Federal Policy for the Protection of
Human Research Subjects,” and issued by 16 federal departments and agencies.4,16
The CFR also became known as the Common Rule and currently is applied to any research that
is conducted or funded by 16 federal departments and agencies.4,16,17
Among the concepts embodied by or underlying the Common Rule are informed consent and
the right to voluntary withdrawal, the need for a well-articulated and testable hypothesis, an
appropriate research design with minimization of risks to subjects, adequate predicate
information to justify a clinical study, an appropriately trained and responsible research team,
independent research committee (institutional review board [IRB]) review and approval of the
project, equitable subject selection, and an appropriate relationship between the risks and
advantages to subjects and the knowledge that may result from the study.4,16,17
Human Tissue Ethical History
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
5/19

One of the most famous cases of human tissue ethics involved the cervical cancer cells of
Henrietta Lacks (1920–1951), an African American woman who was being treated for cervical
cancer at the Johns Hopkins Hospital.
Consent to participate in research was not standard at the time. Her tumor cells, obtained
from biopsies performed during treatment, were taken for research without her consent and
placed in tissue culture.4,18-20
They exhibited a property of multiple replications without dying and were termed
immortalized. They became known as HeLa cells.4,18-20
HeLa cells have been widely distributed to laboratories throughout the country and have
been used for research on cancer, AIDS, toxicity studies, gene mapping, cloning, and the
development of the polio vaccine.4,18-20
More than 10,000 patents have been included in research performed with HeLa cells.4,18-20
Ms. Lacks’ physicians did not seek her consent before using her tissues for research, but they
did not receive any personal financial gain from the cell line.4,18-20
The cell line did become extremely lucrative financially, and genetically modified versions of
the cell line currently sell for as much as $10,000.4,18-20
The Lacks family has never received any financial benefits from the HeLa cell line.4,18-20
Another instance of ethical controversy over human tissue involves WI-38 cells.4,21
These cells, commonly used in vaccine production around the world since the mid 1960s,
were derived from the lung tissue of a surgically aborted fetus.4,21
Although the figures cannot be accurately determined, it is probable that the commercial
sale of vaccines produced with WI-38 cells is valued in the multiple billions of dollars.4,21
One of the major sources of ethical guidelines in this realm comes from the case of Moore
versus the Regents of the University of California.
In 1976, John Moore was treated at the University of California–Los Angeles Medical Center
for leukemia, a treatment that included a splenectomy.4,22
Preoperatively, his physician had determined that he was going to use portions of Moore’s
spleen in research activities he was conducting, but he did not inform Moore about those
intentions.4,22
Moore signed a standard surgical consent form for the therapeutic procedure, but the form
did not include consent for the use of the surgically removed tissue for research.4,22
In subsequent visits, blood samples were obtained, some of which may have been used for
research.4,22
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
6/19

Cell cultures were developed with Moore’s tissues and, in 1984, a patent was issued to the
University of California for a Mo cell line that was developed from these cultures.4,22
In collaboration with Genetics Institute and Sandoz Pharmaceutical, several products were
developed from the Mo cell line.4,22
The case raised several issues, dealt with separately by several California courts, including
whether individuals have the right to be informed about how biospecimens obtained from
them will be used and whether individuals from whom biospecimens are obtained have
patent or financial rights to methods, services, or products subsequently developed from
their tissues.4,22
The California Supreme Court held that in circumstances in which a physician is pursuing
research activities that may affect the physician’s professional judgment, an explicit duty
existed to obtain informed consent to those activities, which may include consent to use
biospecimens for research.4,22
The court recognized that the dual role of the physician as a healer and a researcher
created an inherent conflict of interest for the physician and imposed an obligation for the
physician/researcher to disclose that conflict of interest, including potentially profiting from
the research, if such profit existed.4,22
However, the court also held that Moore did not have a property interest in his removed
tissues.4,22
In a penetrating analysis, the court wrote “It is important to realize that patent rights are
only available to the inventor who reduces his idea to practice. ‘Products of nature,’ no
matter how exceptional, cannot be the subject of patent protection. Thus, patent
protection is not available for human tissue in its unaltered form, and the fact that patent
protection has been granted to the inventor of a cell-line (or other genetically engineered
substance) has no bearing on what rights the source of the original tissue may possess in
that tissue.”4,22
Other legal precedents have supported the view that patients do not have a property
interest in tissues used for research.4,22
Payment for biospecimens is one of the largest current debates in research ethics.
The two major questions are whether patients should be paid for their tissues and whether
patients should share in the monetary gain generated for research, including salaries, funds
to institutions, intellectual property, patents, products, or medical devices.4,20,23
One argument states that the value generated is more attributable to the experiment and
the research process.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
7/19

The other argument states that biological tissues have inherent, independent value.4,20,23
This debate was explored in a related Policy Forum that was published in the journal, Science,
in 2012.4,20,23
Financial compensation was held to be unnecessary if biospecimens were obtained
incidental to needed care, but compensation was considered appropriate if biospecimen
donation imposed added effort, burden, or risk.4,20
In keeping with the Moore decision,4,22 payments in these cases are made for the
performance of a service rather than for a transfer of property (the biospecimens).4,20
The authors would deny patients a right to payment for research that yields profits, based
on the legal norms that tissues separated from the body are not the ongoing property of
the individual.4,20
Rather, it is the researchers, not the patients, whose intellectual efforts lead to the creation
of value.4,20
Other investigators have taken a different view and have expressed support for payment
for biospecimens.4,23
Evolution of Ethical Guidelines
Updating the Belmont Report
Five themes for possible revision of the report have been identified: (1) the distinctions
between clinical research and clinical practice, (2) the harms to communities, (3) the
transparency of research activities, (4) the implications of protectionism, and (5) the
relationship between the ethical principles of the Belmont Report and their applications.4,24
“The Belmont Report was an impressive and inspiring response to the ethical issues of its day.
Since its release, the field of research involving human subjects has developed in complex and
unexpected ways, challenging the report’s ethical framework to respond to not only the fears
related to research abuses that it stemmed from, but also to the increasing commodification
of bio-medicine, the exclusion of many groups from research, the globalization of research,
the desires of many to have access to experimental drugs, the lack of generalizability and
reproducibility of many research findings, and the unique harms and histories that
communities have experienced as a result of research.”4,24
Updates to the Common Rule
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
8/19

In 2009, the Federal Office of Management and Budget created a group to examine and
propose revisions to the Common Rule.4,25
In 2011, the group released an advanced notice of proposed rulemaking.4,26
The document explained the need for updating the regulations as follows: “The current
regulations governing human subjects research were developed years ago when research
was predominantly conducted at universities, colleges, and medical institutions, and each
study generally took place at only a single site. Although the regulations have been amended
over the years, they have not kept pace with the evolving human research enterprise, the
proliferation of multi-site clinical trials and observational studies, the expansion of health
services research, research in the social and behavioral sciences, and research involving
databases, the Internet, and biological specimen repositories, and the use of advanced
technologies, such as genomics.”4,26
This work evolved into a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that was signed and released for
public comment in September 2015.4,27
Various specific changes were suggested that centered around two main themes: eliminating
inappropriate barriers to the conduct of research that were imposed by current regulations
(such as administrative burdens that did not substantively contribute to subject well-being)
and increasing protections for subjects in circumstances that were appropriate or
necessary.4,27
After public commentary and debate, a final rule was released in 2017, and the changes were
enacted and enforced between January 2019 and January 2020.4,28
The most important changes to the Common Rule centered around informed consent and
improvements in the process of educating prospective subjects about the risks and
advantages of enrolling in a study.4,28 The following six key changes were recommended.
Prospective subjects must be given the information that “a reasonable person would want to
have to make an informed decision” about whether to participate.4,28 A reasonable person
standard is a standard that has long been used in the law for determining what information
to provide when a doctor obtains consent for clinical care.4,28 It is viewed as the more ethical
standard than the competing professional standard, which requires physicians and other
caregivers to disclose only the information that they think a patient needs to know.4,28
The information must be provided “in sufficient detail relating to the research.”4,28 This
change was made in response to the often vague information in current consent forms
about what may happen to someone in a research study, even though more specific
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
9/19

information exists that may be very helpful.4,28 For example, the section of a cancer clinical
trial consent form discussing the possible benefits from participating may merely state that
an individual may or may not benefit.4,28 However, knowing that the possible benefit would,
at best, be a reduction of pain but not any alteration in how long a patient may survive would
be important information that should be provided.4,28
Importantly, consent “must begin with a concise and focused presentation of the key
information that is most likely to assist a prospective subject...in understanding the reasons
why one might or might not want to participate in the research.”4,28 This change was made in
recognition that consent forms have been getting longer and longer and that the information
that may be most useful to prospective subjects is buried inside less important
information.4,28 As a result of this new requirement, even if a consent form is long, at least
the first few pages contain the information most helpful to the subject in making a decision
about participation.4,28
A new requirement that applies to the concise presentation at the beginning of the consent
form and the consent form as a whole is that the information “must be organized and
presented in a way that facilitates comprehension.”4,28 Therefore, rather than presenting
separate discussions of advantages, risks, and alternatives, a consent form may discuss the
interrelationships of these elements and how those interrelationships may be relevant to a
person’s decision about participation.4,28
A new element was added to the basic elements of informed consent, and three new
elements were added to the additional elements of informed consent.4,28
The new basic element requires that, in research involving the collection of identifiable
private information or identifiable biospecimens, prospective subjects must be informed
about the possibility that identifiers can be removed from the information or biospecimens,
after which additional research can take place without consent.4,28 As an alternative to
providing such a statement, the consent form can include a promise to not conduct such
research with de-identified information or biospecimens.4,28
The first new additional element requires informing prospective subjects about the
possibility of their biospecimens being used for commercial profit, if indeed that may
happen.4,28 It also requires telling the subjects whether they would share in such profit.4,28
A second element requires telling subjects whether clinically relevant research results
(including results specific to the subject) will be shared with them, and if so, under what
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
10/19

circumstances.4,28 The third new element is a disclosure about whether research with
biospecimens may include whole genome sequencing.4,28
The final rule also adopted new provisions for a type of broad consent involving a person
providing consent to unspecified future secondary research with identifiable private
information or identifiable biospecimens.4,28 Secondary research means research involving
information or biospecimens that were initially collected for some other primary purpose.4,28
Although rules governing broad consent were initially proposed in the 2015 Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, the reason for proposing them again largely related to the new
requirement for obtaining informed consent before conducting research with nonidentified
biospecimens.4,27,28 Because that consent requirement was not adopted, the new broad
consent rules end up instead serving as a voluntary option that supplements the existing
(and largely unchanged) manners in which secondary research can take place.4,28
In addition to revising and improving the informed consent process, numerous other changes
occurred.4,28
Some activities conducted by or at the request of government entities would no longer be
classified as research and, therefore, would no longer be subject to the Common Rule.
Public health surveillance activities that are conducted by or at the request of a public
health authority4,28
Scholarly and journalistic activities (oral history, journalism, biography, literary criticism,
legal research, and historical scholarship) that focus directly on the specific individuals
about whom the information is collected4,28
The proposals to expand the exemption provisions and create some new exemptions were
adopted in many respects but with some important changes.
A new exemption category for certain types of research that involves only benign
behavioral interventions was created.4,28
The category of survey and related research was expanded to allow the collection of
sensitive private information; however, such research would need to undergo limited IRB
review for the purpose of verifying that appropriate privacy and confidentiality provisions
were put in place.4,28
The two proposed exemptions for the storage and secondary research use of certain
biospecimens and identifiable private information were adopted; however, they only apply
to identifiable biospecimens because the proposal relating to nonidentified biospecimens
was not adopted.4,28
Various forms of limited IRB review are required to qualify for the exemptions.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
11/19

The proposed exemption related to providing notice of certain types of secondary research
was not adopted; however, a different exemption about the research use of identifiable
health information that was subject to certain Health Insurance Portability and
Accountability Act of 1996 protections was adopted.4,28
A few IRB-centric proposals were adopted in the most recent changes.4,28
The proposal that required one IRB that serves as the IRB of record for all multi-
institutional research conducted by United States institutions within the United States was
adopted.4,28
The proposal to eliminate the requirement of continuing annual IRB review of research was
adopted.4,28
Modern Ethical Standards
Ethical Study Design
In crafting a study, the investigator should first consider the guiding principles that were
outlined in the Belmont Report, namely respect for persons and their autonomy, beneficence,
and justice1,4,15,29-31 (Resource 3).
Patients should be well-informed about the risks and advantages of participation and the
objectives of the study.1,4,15,29-31
The study should optimize the potential beneficial outcomes and minimize risks to the
subjects involved.1,4,15,29-31
Studies should have sound reasoning as their basis, should not be exploitative in nature, and
should be conducted fairly.1,4,15,29-31
Informed Consent
A true informed consent requires three key elements: provision of adequate information,
comprehension of the information by the person being asked to consent, and voluntariness.
An appropriate informed consent depends on providing information so the patient can
decide whether to enroll in a research study.29-31
The risks and advantages of enrolling in the study should be clearly communicated without
using medical jargon.29-31
It is important to discuss certain points with the patient, including alternative options, that
not enrolling in the study will not affect their clinical care, and that the patient can withdraw
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
12/19

from the study at any time.29-31
Communication should be written and oral, and the physician obtaining consent should
make a good faith effort to evaluate whether the patient understands the information that
has been provided.29-31
Industry Relationships
Relationships between medical professionals and industry are not intrinsically bad; however,
they can expose those involved in conflicts of interest.29-32
As in clinical practice, physicians conducting research must disclose any relationships they
have with industry, including employment, scientific collaborations, clinical relationships, and
marketing collaborations.29-32
Industry can sponsor physician-led research; however, the funding source should be
disclosed to the subjects.29-32
Physician-investigators and those involved in writing the research manuscript should request
access to raw data from the project; however, this step is not an industry research
normative.29-32
Industry relationships also can risk bias in the research, especially when or if compensation
is tied to particular research outcomes.29-32
If a research contract is established, the setting of the physician-investigator’s practice may
add complexity to the research arrangement.29-32
In academic medical centers, research contracts generally are agreements made between
the institution and the company, whereas in private practice, the contract usually is made
between the practice and the sponsor or contract research organization.29-32
Contracts with academic medical centers are more complicated because universities, as
nonprofit entities, must work in the public benefit.29-32
In research, that requirement usually means assurance that the work will be published.29-32
Many academic medical centers include language in their contracts that allows them to
retain the rights to new intellectual property.29-32
Because private practices rarely pay attention to these issues, those practices have
contractual advantages from the point of view of many sponsors.29-32
If an NIH grant is involved, the United States Public Health Service requires reporting of all
major financial interests that may directly and substantially affect the design, conduct, or
reporting of research.29-33
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:00 PM
AAOS | Research Ethics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001011
13/19

This responsibility falls on the institution that receives the grant, usually an academic
institution or nonprofit organization.29-33
To help the institution identify which financial interests to report, investigators are required
to fully disclose their financial relationships.29-33
After those relationships are disclosed to the institution, the conflict-of-interest program is
expected to manage any conflicts.29-33
Typical management strategies include a requirement for the disclosure of external financial
relationships.29-33
IRBs often require that informed consent documents provide information about external
financial interests.29-33
The NIH expects the institution to describe how its management approach will mitigate the
effects of conflict-of-interest–related bias in the research.29-33
The institution is required to file a formal report with the United States Public Health
Service.29-33
Recent legislation in the form of the 2013 Physician Payments Sunshine Act (which is a
component of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010) requires
pharmaceutical companies, device manufacturers, and medical service providers to report all
payments of $10 or more made to physicians and academic medical centers.29-32,34
These reports will be summarized in a publicly accessible, searchable website so all
physician-industry financial arrangements become public knowledge.29-32,34
Institutional Review Boards
The function of an IRB is to evaluate research protocols for scientific validity, ethical design,
and proposed conduct.17,29-31
IRB regulation and approval of research is required for federally sponsored research because
of the CFR.17,29-31
Specifically, regulation 45 CFR §46, which is known as the Common Rule described
previously, is applied to most human investigation or research in the United States.17,29-31
If the FDA is involved, they have their own set of rules, which are set down in regulation 21
CFR §50 and §56 and are similar to the Common Rule but add requirements related to FDA
jurisdiction.29,35,36
Before human subjects are enrolled in a research study in the United States, the research
proposal should be submitted to an IRB for review and approval by that body.17,29-31

Summary
Orthopaedic surgeons should understand the evolution of contemporary ethical and legal
thinking governing experimentation with human subjects, including key features of design of a
modern ethical study.
The history of medical ethics has many examples of improper and harmful behavior,
including the study of yellow fever in Cuba and by Walter Reed,1-3 the experiments
conducted by the Nazis,4,5 and the Tuskegee Syphilis Study.4,12-14
In response to these ethical violations, multiple sets of guidelines were established, including
the Belmont Report1,4,15 and the current guidelines included in the CFR (most recently
updated in 2017).4,16,17,28,29,35,36
The three main principles that guide ethical medical research—which are derived from the
Belmont Report—are respect for persons and their autonomy, beneficence, and
justice.1,4,15,29-31
Studies must be designed with these guiding principles in mind and orthopaedic surgeons
must work within the currently established legal framework to optimize the amount of useful
information obtained from studies while ensuring maximum protections for the subjects
enrolled.4
Because clinical science is dynamic, ethical and legal frameworks will need to continue to
evolve along with clinical techniques and technologies.4
Mark as Complete
